These guidelines help Procurement teams evaluate commercial and operational considerations when acquiring AI-enabled products or services. They are guidance and do not replace corporate policy, security standards, or approval authority.

Procurement should identify the provider, commercial model, expected users, intended business use, data categories, integration requirements, support model, portability, termination provisions, and material subcontractors.

Commercial review should consider service commitments, data-processing terms, retention options, intellectual-property provisions, model or service changes, audit rights where applicable, and exit requirements.

These guidelines do not authorize a new AI tool. Formal approval is governed by the AI Governance Policy and Approval Authority Matrix. Information Security determines applicable security requirements.
The fact that an AI product is procured does not mean confidential supplier or customer data may automatically be entered into it. Data classification and approved-use requirements remain applicable.

fields.text: This active corporate policy establishes transportation service targets and escalation governance. It supersedes DOC-002, Transportation Policy v2.0 (2024). Where historical values differ, the active policy governs current operations. Applies to domestic transportation operations, including contracted carriers and business-critical deliveries. Detailed operational procedures remain in DOC-003 and DOC-009.

OTIF (On Time In Full) measures deliveries that are both on time and in full divided by total deliveries. The national target is 97% from 2026-01-01. The prior target was 95% through 2025-12-31; the change was approved during 2025. OTIF definition and additional carrier performance indicators are maintained in DOC-013. Operational source systems remain authoritative for actual delivery records.

Standard: delivery within 5 business days after dispatch; Express: within 2 business days; Critical: the approved commitment specified in the critical-delivery record, with an initial target of next business day when operationally feasible. On-time status is assessed against the documented category commitment. No service category overrides an approved exception or a more specific signed contract.

A critical delivery is a shipment explicitly classified as business-critical under the active Critical Delivery SOP (DOC-009). Classification must be recorded; urgency alone does not automatically qualify. Delayed critical deliveries require the defined escalation workflow in DOC-009. The policy establishes this obligation but does not replace the SOP's detailed qualifying criteria, contacts, and deadlines.

Repeated SLA breach for three consecutive weeks requires escalation under DOC-003. Carrier replacement, corrective actions and performance review are governed by DOC-003 and applicable contracts. Exceptions must be documented, time-limited and approved by the designated owner. Historical documents may be consulted for context but are not current operational authority.
Related sources: DOC-002 (superseded historical policy), DOC-003 (Carrier Management Policy), DOC-009 (Critical Delivery SOP), DOC-013 (Logistics KPI Dictionary), DOC-019 (2025 committee minutes).

Confidential customer information may be transmitted to an authorized external party only when there is a legitimate business purpose, the recipient is authorized, and an approved secure transfer mechanism or controlled platform is used.

Ordinary email transmission to an external recipient is not an approved mechanism for confidential customer information unless the enterprise has explicitly approved the technical protection and process for that use case. A legacy operational instruction permitting routine email transmission does not override this policy.

Confidential information must not be entered into an AI tool unless that tool and use case are approved for the relevant information classification. Required controls include approved access, data handling terms, identity and access management, logging where applicable, and compliance with AI governance requirements.

Accidental disclosure, unauthorized transmission, or suspected exposure of confidential information must be reported and handled under the active Security Incident SOP. Employees must not attempt to conceal or independently resolve a material disclosure without reporting it.

Where an SOP, work instruction, local guide, or historical document conflicts with this policy, the conflict must be resolved according to the Document Governance Policy. Lower-authority documents cannot weaken corporate security requirements.

fields.text: Document ID: DOC-023 | Version: 1.0 | Effective: 2026-01-01 | Status: ACTIVE | Type: Corporate Policy
Establish governance requirements for selecting, approving, and using AI systems in enterprise work while preserving human accountability, information protection, and traceability.

Employees may use approved AI tools for legitimate business purposes within the approved use case and data classification. Approval of a tool does not automatically approve every data type or business decision.

AI may be used to summarize or analyze supplier contracts only when the tool and use case are approved, applicable confidentiality requirements are satisfied, and the output is treated as analytical support rather than authoritative legal interpretation.

Use of supplier data in AI requires an approved AI tool/use case, compliance with the Data Sharing Policy and Information Security Policy, and the approvals applicable to the data classification. Confidential supplier data additionally requires Information Security and AI Governance approval as defined by the Approval Authority Matrix.

A new AI tool that processes enterprise or supplier data requires approval by the AI Governance Owner, with Information Security and Procurement review. Additional review may be required for legal, privacy, regulated, or high-impact use cases.

AI-generated analysis or recommendations do not transfer decision accountability from the authorized human role. Decisions requiring formal approval remain subject to the relevant authority matrix and business policy.
Users must complete the required AI workforce training before using approved AI tools for enterprise work and must complete role-specific modules when assigned.
AI Security Standard; AI Workforce Enablement Guide; Information Security Policy; Data Sharing Policy; Approval Authority Matrix.

Legal entity registration and tax status; transport operating authorization when applicable; insurance certificate and coverage schedule; bank and payment registration; signed confidentiality/data-processing agreement; safety/compliance declarations; named operational and escalation contacts; executed commercial contract.

Procurement receives documents and records completeness; Compliance validates legal and risk information; Transportation validates service capability; Information Security validates data-sharing arrangements; the authorized approver releases the supplier under DOC-012.
Missing mandatory documentation prevents activation unless an approved, recorded exception applies. Retain document versions, reviewer decisions and approval timestamp.

fields.text: Provide a repeatable workflow for classifying, monitoring and escalating critical deliveries. Applies to domestic transportation operations and contracted carriers.

Classify a delivery as critical when at least one documented condition applies: (a) imminent interruption of a business-critical operation; (b) contractual or regulatory deadline with material consequence; (c) emergency replacement of essential equipment; or (d) explicit approval by the accountable Operations Manager based on documented business impact.

The requester records shipment ID, business impact, required delivery deadline, approving owner and recovery contact. A delivery is not critical solely because it is late or marked urgent in free text.
Step 1 — Requester records the classification reason and deadline.
Step 2 — Operations validates eligibility and confirms the accountable owner.
Step 3 — Transportation Control Tower records the commitment and carrier acknowledgement.
Step 4 — Monitor checkpoints and update the case log until proof of delivery or formal exception closure.

At predicted or confirmed breach: notify Control Tower immediately and open an incident record. Within 30 minutes, notify Operations Manager and carrier escalation contact. Within 60 minutes, obtain a documented recovery ETA and alternative routing or capacity option.
If the recovery ETA cannot meet the approved critical commitment, escalate to Transportation Management and the affected business owner for a documented mitigation decision.
Close only after proof of delivery or a documented exception decision. Record event timeline, root cause, recovery actions, decision owner and any corrective-action reference.
Authority references: DOC-001 (active Transportation Policy), DOC-003 (Carrier Management Policy), DOC-013 (KPI Dictionary).

Define the immediate response and escalation process for suspected or confirmed information-security incidents, including accidental disclosure to suppliers.

Use this SOP when confidential or restricted information may have been sent to an unauthorized recipient, transmitted through an unapproved channel, exposed through an approved system, or otherwise handled contrary to policy.
Stop further disclosure where feasible without destroying evidence.
Notify the Information Security incident channel immediately.
Record what information was involved, recipient, transmission method, time, and known scope.
Do not instruct the external recipient to delete evidence before Information Security provides direction.
Preserve relevant messages, logs, files, and screenshots.
Follow containment, notification, and remediation instructions issued by the incident owner.

If confidential data was accidentally sent to a supplier or carrier, the employee must report the incident immediately. Information Security coordinates containment and determines whether Procurement, Legal, Privacy, the business owner, or the supplier must take additional action.
An incident is closed only after the responsible incident owner records containment, impact assessment, required notifications, remediation, and follow-up actions.
Information Security Policy; Data Sharing Policy; applicable supplier agreement.
